metadata.title: Zeeman Crossover — Hydrogen 2p Manifold, Judged
metadata.purpose: viz-riff critique of the Zeeman crossover energy-level diagram

beats.narration_text: Hola, Liam — in for Bear. An educator asks: hey Claude, write me a visualization of the Zeeman crossover in hydrogen's 2p manifold. Here's what comes back. Today we judge the viz, not the physics.

props.command: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for the Zeeman crossover in hydrogen's 2p manifold.

beats.narration_text: The chart shows six curves plotted against B field from zero to five tesla. The y-axis carries the label Energy times ten to the minus five electron-volts; ticks run from negative fifty to positive fifty as plain numbers. One curve is red at a heavier stroke weight. Three are thin solid black. Two are thin gray dashed. A red dashed vertical line marks B-critical at 0.78 tesla. Two horizontal reference lines mark the fine-structure splitting. Regime text labels near the bottom edge read Anomalous Zeeman on the left and Paschen-Back on the right. A side panel shows a color-coded regime badge and a live table of six state labels with numeric energy values. Moving dots mark each state at the current field value. A slider at the bottom controls B.
beats.new_visual_element: SOURCE-CUT: media/B01.mp4 (output.mp4 — baseline at B=0.5T, all six states visible)

beats.narration_text: The slider drives B from zero to five tesla. At each position the code calls computeEigenvalues — an analytic two-by-two diagonalization in the m-j equals plus or minus one-half blocks. The six dots update instantly. At B-critical the side panel badge flips from cream to red: the code tests whether B is less than Bc for the anomalous Zeeman regime and greater for Paschen-Back. The question the viewer is supposed to answer: watch the curves fan out — do the j equals one-half and j equals three-halves states fully separate in the strong-field limit?
beats.new_visual_element: SOURCE-CUT: media/B02.mp4 (change.mp4 — full B sweep 0→5T, badge flips at Bc)

beats.narration_text: Three things work. First: the crossover threshold is made unavoidable by three co-operating encodings — the red vertical line at Bc, the badge that switches color at that exact moment, and the regime text in the background. A student cannot miss that something changes at 0.78 tesla. Second: the dashed lines for j equals one-half states map the j quantum number to a perceptual channel beyond color, so the two spin-orbit families stay visually separable even for a viewer with color deficiency. Third: the live numeric table acts as a calculator — set a specific B value, read exact energies, check them against the equation.

shot.note: CALLOUT OVERLAY (final pass): ring the Bc vertical line, circle badge at flip moment

beats.new_visual_element: SOURCE-CUT: media/B03.mp4 (change.mp4 t=0–6s — crossover approach, badge flip at ~1.8s)

beats.narration_text: Three problems. Most dangerous: the y-axis ticks show bare numbers — minus twenty-five, plus fifty — and the exponent lives only in the axis label as a tiny prefix. A student who skims past that prefix thinks these are electron-volt-scale energies, five orders of magnitude wrong. The fix: put the unit directly on each tick. Second: the five non-red curves have no labels on the chart itself. In the Paschen-Back regime you cannot identify any line without memorizing the side panel table. Third: the side panel keeps j and m-j labels at five tesla, where the good quantum numbers are m-l and m-s. The visualization teaches the wrong eigenbasis across the majority of its slider range.

shot.note: CALLOUT OVERLAY (final pass): circle y-axis exponent label, point at unlabeled curves, highlight |j,mj⟩ labels in panel

beats.new_visual_element: SOURCE-CUT: media/B04.mp4 (change.mp4 t=5.5–11.5s — deep Paschen-Back, fanned curves, wrong state labels)

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Clear threshold encoding: Bc is marked three ways and cannot be missed. Dual-channel legend — dash encodes j, not just color — so the families stay separable. But y-axis ticks that hide their exponent. No on-chart curve labels past the red line. State labels that use the wrong quantum numbers above Bc. Best use: show this in lecture at the phase-transition moment. One fix matters most: put the exponent on each tick so the energy scale is honest at first glance.

props.artifactHeading: When to use it, and what to fix.
artifactLines: Three-way Bc encoding: line + badge + label. Unavoidable.
Dash-encodes j family — separable without color.
Y-axis ticks hide the ×10⁻⁵ exponent. Five orders of magnitude wrong.
One fix: put the exponent on each tick.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. I have a D3 visualization of the Zeeman crossover in hydrogen's 2p manifold. I need three fixes. One: rescale the y-axis so each tick shows its value directly in units of ten to the minus five eV — for example minus 2.25 — rather than raw-domain numbers that require a hidden exponent in the axis label. Two: in the Paschen-Back regime above Bc, relabel each curve on the chart with its dominant m-l and m-s quantum numbers rather than j and m-j. Three: add hover labels to each of the six curves so a student can identify any line without consulting the side panel. Keep the single-file D3 format and return the modified HTML.

props.command: I have a D3 visualization of the Zeeman crossover in hydrogen's 2p manifold. Fix three things. One: rescale the y-axis so each tick shows the value in units of 10⁻⁵ eV directly (e.g. −2.25) — not raw-domain numbers that need a hidden exponent. Two: in the Paschen-Back regime (B > Bc), relabel each curve on the chart with its dominant mₗ, mₛ quantum numbers instead of j, mⱼ. Three: add hover labels to all six curves so a student can identify any line without the side panel. Keep single-file D3 format.

beats.narration_text: Zeeman Crossover — weak field to Paschen-Back, judged. Liam, in for Bear.
